newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura down, but not out for count -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: Nomura down, but not out for count -- analysts.

text.p: Giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd, battered by a widening racketeer payoff scandal, faces a long, tough battle to repair its credibility with clients.
But several analysts said the brokerage was still likely to emerge a winner in Tokyo's increasingly competitive markets.

Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki was arrested on Friday on suspicion of conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen in 1995 to Ryuichi Koike, a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the scandal.
The three other executives, Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori have already been arrested.
"I think it (the arrest) is another nail in the coffin of Nomura's reputation," said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSBC James Capel.

"Clearly, the new issues from which they are being excluded and the amount of business they are losing is hurting them financially, and it takes a long, long time to rebuild client confidence and get your reputation back," Waterhouse said.
In the latest client defections, officials at several major Japanese electric power companies said on Friday they had excluded Nomura from the underwriting syndicates for their latest bond issues.
Waterhouse and other analysts, however, said Nomura still looked well-placed to succeed down the road as Japan moves to deregulate its financial markets over the next five years.

"Longer term, I still think Nomura will be one of the few winners in the 'Big Bang'. But it seems clear that they will have to make radical changes to their operations, their management structure and disclosure, and improve accountability," Waterhouse said.
Nomura is more vulnerable to losing business or rivals than in the past given the rise of viable competitors, including foreign brokerages.
The longer the scandal lasts, with its accompanying uncertainty over penalties and punishments, the more business the brokerage is likely to lose.

"It's dragging on and that's the worst possible scenario for Nomura," said James Fiorillo, analyst at ING Barings Securities (Japan). "Clients are waiting for a final resolution from the Finance Ministry and the prosecutors."
But Fiorillo agreed that it was too soon to write Nomura off as a big player in Japanese markets post-Big Bang.
"Everyone is chiselling out a gravestone, but I'm not," he said.
